newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Fifty dead as Russian plane to Turkey crashes.
newsitem.headline: Fifty dead as Russian plane to Turkey crashes.

text.p: Fifty passengers and crew aboard a Russian airliner died when it crashed on Tuesday en route to Turkey, officials said.
It was the worst domestic disaster for Russia's troubled airline industry in more than a year.

Pyotr Markin, an assistant to the airline's director, said by telephone that the charter Stavropol Airlines AN-24 crashed 37 minutes after taking off from Stavropol in south Russia for Trabzon on Turkey's northern coast.
"We believe the plane caught fire in mid air and fell into a forest," said Vladimir Konnonov, the duty officer of the local emergency committee.
"Rescue teams say nobody survived."
Markin said there were 41 passengers and nine crew on board.
"Air traffic control did not receive any information from the crew about any dangers, but then the plane disappeared from the radar screen, ending communications," Markin said.
By late afternoon rescuers had recovered 24 bodies scattered across a large snow-covered field, Sergei Berezin, deputy mayor of Cherkessk near the crash site, said by telephone.
Markin said the plane's flight recorder had also been found in good condition.

Interfax news agency quoted regional governor Vladimir Khubiyev as saying the accident could have been caused by an explosion on board. Witnesses "heard a boom and saw the tail of the plane begin to separate already in the air," he said.
Zulfa Batasheva, a regional public prosecutor, told Reuters the tail was found 1.5 km (one mile) away from the rest of the wreck, raising the possibility that the plane fell apart in midair.
However local police official Murat Baibagisov, contacted by telephone, said an eyewitness with whom he spoke saw no explosion, just smoke.
NTV commercial television showed film of the bodies. Much of the twisted wreckage was piled high in a snow-covered forest, although the tail was in a large field.
Markin said it was too early to comment on the cause of the crash near the North Caucasus town of Cherkessk, capital of the ethnic region of Karachayevo-Cherkessiya.
But he ruled out the weather -- it was snowing at the time of the crash -- as a factor.
Officials said most if not all passengers were Russian "shuttle traders" who buy goods abroad to resell at home.
Russia's air safety standards have fallen since Soviet monopoly Aeroflot was split into hundreds of smaller domestic companies after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Experts say many of the new domestic airlines are struggling financially, forcing some to take shortcuts in maintenence and safety standards.
Aviation officials say 219 people died last year in 43 air accidents in Russian air space.
The crash was the worst in Russia since December 1995, when 97 died in an air disaster in the Russian Far East. The crash of a Vnukovo Airlines flight in Norway killed 140 last August.
